q: You create a container app with HTTP ingress and don't define any scale settings. What scaling behavior does the app get?
o: The default HTTP rule with a minimum of 0 and a maximum of 10 replicas per revision
A fixed single replica that never scales
A minimum of 1 and a maximum of 100 replicas
No scaling until you add a KEDA rule
e: If no scale rule is defined, Container Apps applies the default HTTP scale rule with 0 minimum replicas and 10 maximum replicas per revision, so the app can scale to zero when idle. You can raise the maximum up to 1,000. Replicas are scaled automatically, so no extra rule is required for HTTP traffic.

q: An HTTP scale rule is added without specifying concurrentRequests. At roughly what load does Container Apps add another replica?
o: About 10 concurrent requests per replica, the default
About 100 concurrent requests per replica
When CPU reaches 80 percent
When memory reaches 80 percent
e: The HTTP scale rule's concurrentRequests defaults to 10 (minimum 1). Concurrency is calculated every 15 seconds as the requests in the past 15 seconds divided by 15. CPU and memory thresholds are separate custom rule types and aren't the default.

q: A worker uses a custom KEDA rule on a Service Bus queue with minReplicas 0. After the queue empties, the last replica keeps running for about five minutes before the app scales to zero. Why?
o: Custom rules have a 300-second cool-down period that applies when scaling in from the final replica to 0
KEDA polls the queue only once every 5 minutes
Service Bus keeps messages locked for 5 minutes
Scale-to-zero is not supported for Service Bus rules
e: Custom scale rules use a 30-second polling interval and a 300-second cool-down period, and the cool-down applies only when scaling in from the final replica to zero. That's why the app waits about five minutes after the queue reaches zero. Service Bus scaling does support scale to zero, and the polling interval is 30 seconds, not 5 minutes.

q: You want a container app to scale on the length of the Service Bus queue orders, adding a replica for every 5 messages and authenticating with a connection string kept in a secret named sb-conn. Which CLI parameters are correct?
o: --scale-rule-type azure-servicebus --scale-rule-metadata "queueName=orders" "namespace=contoso-sb" "messageCount=5" --scale-rule-auth "connection=sb-conn"
--scale-rule-http-concurrency 5 --secrets sb-conn
--scale-rule-type cpu --scale-rule-metadata "value=5"
--scale-rule-type servicebus-queue --scale-rule-auth "sb-conn"
e: Custom rules use the KEDA scaler type (azure-servicebus), its metadata as key=value pairs (queue name, namespace, and messageCount as the target per replica), and --scale-rule-auth to map the scaler's connection trigger parameter to a secret. HTTP concurrency and CPU rules don't read queue length, and servicebus-queue isn't the KEDA scaler name.

q: You want a Service Bus scale rule to authenticate with the app's managed identity instead of a connection string. In the Azure portal you can't find the option. What should you do?
o: Configure the rule with the CLI (--scale-rule-identity) or with Bicep/ARM (identity in the custom rule), because the portal doesn't support managed identity for scale rules
Create the rule as an HTTP rule instead
Give the identity Contributor on the container app
Managed identity isn't supported for any KEDA scaler in Container Apps
e: Container Apps supports managed identity for the Azure Queue Storage, Service Bus, and Event Hubs scalers, but the portal doesn't expose it; you set it with --scale-rule-identity in the CLI or identity in the custom block of Bicep/ARM. An HTTP rule can't read queue length, and Contributor on the app doesn't authenticate the scaler to Service Bus.

q: A background worker container app has ingress disabled. You set no minReplicas and no custom scale rule. What is the risk?
o: The app can scale to zero and never restart, because nothing will trigger it to scale out again
The app will scale to 1,000 replicas
Revisions will be deactivated every night
The app can't be deployed without ingress
e: Without ingress, the default HTTP rule never fires. Microsoft warns that if ingress is disabled and you define neither minReplicas nor a custom rule, the app scales to zero and has no way to start again. Set minReplicas to 1 or more, or add an event-driven rule such as a queue scaler.

q: A team adds a CPU scale rule to a container app and expects it to scale to zero overnight. It never goes below one replica. Why?
o: CPU and memory scale rules don't allow a container app to scale to zero
CPU rules require a Dedicated workload profile
The cool-down period for CPU rules is 24 hours
CPU rules only work with multiple revision mode
e: CPU and memory are measured inside running replicas, so these rules can't scale to zero; Microsoft recommends preferring HTTP or event-driven rules when possible. CPU rules work on the Consumption plan and in any revision mode, and there's no 24-hour cool-down.

q: A queue rule targets messageCount=5. There are 100 messages waiting and maxReplicas is 10. How many replicas will the revision run when it fully scales out?
o: 10, because the desired count of ceil(100 / 5) = 20 is capped by maxReplicas
20, because maxReplicas is a soft limit
5, because messageCount is the replica limit
100, one replica per message
e: KEDA computes desiredReplicas = ceil(currentMetricValue / targetMetricValue), which is 20 here, but replicas never exceed maxReplicas. messageCount is the target number of messages per replica, not a replica cap.

q: Traffic drops sharply, but your container app keeps its extra replicas for a few minutes before scaling in. What explains this?
o: The scale-down stabilization window of 300 seconds
The scale-up stabilization window of 300 seconds
Revisions in single mode can't scale in
HTTP rules only scale in at midnight
e: Container Apps uses a 0-second scale-up stabilization window and a 300-second scale-down stabilization window, so scale-in happens only after the scale-down conditions have held for 300 seconds. This avoids flapping. Scale-up isn't delayed, and both revision modes support scaling in.

q: A container app in multiple revision mode has two active revisions. Each revision's scale settings use minReplicas 1 and maxReplicas 10. What is the maximum total number of replicas?
o: 20, because scale limits apply per revision
10, because limits apply to the whole app
11, the sum of one minimum and one maximum
1,000, because multiple revision mode removes limits
e: Scale limits define the minimum and maximum number of replicas per revision. With two active revisions each limited to 10, the app can run up to 20 replicas in total. Multiple revision mode doesn't remove these limits.

q: A container app must scale on the number of messages in an Azure Storage queue. Which rule should you add?
o: A custom rule of type azure-queue with queueName and queueLength metadata
An HTTP rule with concurrentRequests set to the queue length
A TCP rule on port 443
A memory rule
e: Container Apps uses KEDA, which provides the azure-queue scaler for Azure Storage queues; queueLength is the target number of messages per replica, and authentication uses a secret or a managed identity. HTTP and TCP rules only measure incoming requests or connections, and memory rules measure resource usage, not queue depth.

q: You are designing scaling for a public HTTP API on Container Apps. Which guidance does Microsoft give?
o: Prefer HTTP scale rules over CPU or memory rules when possible
Always combine CPU and memory rules for APIs
Use a TCP rule for all HTTP APIs
Set minReplicas equal to maxReplicas to disable scaling
e: The scaling tutorial recommends HTTP scale rules over CPU or memory rules where possible, because they react directly to demand and allow scale to zero. TCP rules are for non-HTTP traffic, and fixing minReplicas and maxReplicas removes scaling altogether.

q: A latency-sensitive API on Container Apps must never suffer a cold start, but should still scale out under load. What should you configure?
o: Set minReplicas to 1 or more and keep an HTTP scale rule
Set minReplicas to 0 and lower the polling interval
Set maxReplicas to 1
Remove all scale rules
e: Scale to zero happens only when minReplicas is 0, and the first request after scaling to zero waits for a replica to start. Keeping at least one replica avoids that cold start while the HTTP rule still adds replicas under load. maxReplicas 1 prevents scaling out, and removing rules falls back to the default rule with a minimum of 0.

q: You have an AKS cluster and a manifest file store.yaml that defines Deployments and Services. Which command sequence deploys it?
o: az aks get-credentials --resource-group rg --name aks1, then kubectl apply -f store.yaml
az aks create --manifest store.yaml
kubectl run -f store.yaml without credentials
az acr build --file store.yaml
e: az aks get-credentials downloads credentials and configures kubectl to talk to the cluster, and kubectl apply -f creates or updates every object defined in the manifest. az aks create has no manifest option, kubectl needs cluster credentials, and az acr build builds container images, not Kubernetes objects.

q: A Deployment manifest is rejected with an error that the selector doesn't match the template labels. Which fix is correct?
o: Make spec.selector.matchLabels match the labels in spec.template.metadata.labels
Delete the selector; Kubernetes infers it
Add a Service of type LoadBalancer
Set replicas to 0
e: A Deployment manages the pods whose labels match its selector, so spec.selector.matchLabels must match the pod template's labels; the AKS sample manifests use app: <name> in both places. The selector is required for apps/v1 Deployments, a Service doesn't affect Deployment validation, and replicas has no relation to the error.

q: The store-front Deployment must be reachable from the internet with a public IP, while the product-service Deployment must be reachable only inside the cluster. Which Service types should you use?
o: LoadBalancer for store-front and ClusterIP for product-service
ClusterIP for both
NodePort for product-service and ClusterIP for store-front
LoadBalancer for both
e: A LoadBalancer Service gets an external IP from the Azure load balancer, which is how the AKS quickstart exposes the storefront. ClusterIP, the default, gives a cluster-internal IP only, which is what the backend services use. Swapping them or exposing both publicly breaks the requirement.

q: You push an image to contoso.azurecr.io/store-front:v1. What must the image field in your AKS manifest contain?
o: The full name including the ACR login server: contoso.azurecr.io/store-front:v1
Only store-front:v1; AKS searches attached registries automatically
The registry resource ID
docker.io/store-front:v1
e: Kubernetes pulls exactly the image reference in the manifest, so the AKS tutorial has you update the image names to include your ACR login server. Without it, the runtime looks on Docker Hub. Attaching ACR grants pull permissions but doesn't rewrite image names.

q: Pods in an AKS cluster fail to pull images from your Azure container registry with 401 Unauthorized. The registry isn't ABAC-enabled. What is the recommended fix?
o: Run az aks update --name aks1 --resource-group rg --attach-acr <registry>, which grants AcrPull to the kubelet identity
Enable the registry admin user and create an imagePullSecret with its password
Make the registry public
Give the cluster's control plane identity the Owner role on the registry
e: The AKS-ACR integration assigns the AcrPull role to the managed identity of the cluster's agent pools (the kubelet identity), so nodes can pull without stored credentials. Admin-user pull secrets and public registries are discouraged, and Owner is far more privilege than pulling needs and is assigned to the wrong identity.

q: Your container registry uses attribute-based access control (ABAC) repository permissions. A colleague runs az aks update --attach-acr, but nodes still can't pull. What should you do?
o: Manually assign the Container Registry Repository Reader role to the kubelet managed identity
Run --attach-acr again with the --force flag
Assign AcrPull on the resource group instead of the registry
Switch the AKS cluster to use a service principal
e: ABAC-enabled registries don't honor the classic AcrPull role and don't support the --attach-acr integration. You must assign the Container Registry Repository Reader role to the kubelet identity yourself. Repeating the command or assigning AcrPull at a different scope doesn't help.

q: Your AKS cluster has Linux and Windows node pools. A Linux-based Deployment sometimes gets scheduled onto Windows nodes and fails. What should you add to the pod template?
o: nodeSelector: kubernetes.io/os: linux
replicas: 1
imagePullPolicy: Always
A Service of type ClusterIP
e: A nodeSelector constrains pods to nodes with matching labels, and the AKS sample manifests use kubernetes.io/os: linux so Linux containers only run on Linux nodes. Replica count, pull policy, and Services don't affect which operating system a pod is scheduled on.

q: You need to deploy the same manifest into a separate namespace called aks-store-demo. Which commands are correct?
o: kubectl create ns aks-store-demo, then kubectl apply -n aks-store-demo -f manifest.yaml
kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml --cluster aks-store-demo
az aks nodepool add --name aks-store-demo
kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml; namespaces are created from the file name
e: You create the namespace and then use -n (or metadata.namespace in the manifest) to deploy into it, as in the AKS Automatic quickstart. --cluster selects a kubeconfig cluster, not a namespace, a node pool is compute capacity rather than a namespace, and kubectl never derives a namespace from a file name.

q: You change the image tag of a Deployment in its manifest from v1 to v2 and run kubectl apply again. What happens by default?
o: The Deployment performs a rolling update, replacing pods gradually with pods that run v2
All pods are deleted at once and recreated
Nothing changes until you delete the Deployment
A second Deployment is created alongside the first
e: kubectl apply updates the existing Deployment object, and the default RollingUpdate strategy creates new pods from the updated template while scaling down old ones, which avoids downtime. Deployments don't need to be deleted to update, and apply updates the existing object rather than creating a duplicate.

q: A container in AKS is repeatedly killed, and kubectl describe pod shows the last state as OOMKilled. What is the most likely cause?
o: The container exceeds its memory limit, so the limit or the app's memory usage must be adjusted
The image tag doesn't exist in the registry
The liveness probe path is wrong
The Service selector doesn't match the pods
e: OOMKilled means the container used more memory than its limit allowed, and Kubernetes terminated it; incorrect resource limits are a documented cause of CrashLoopBackOff. A missing tag causes ImagePullBackOff, a bad liveness probe shows probe failures in events, and a selector mismatch affects routing, not memory.

q: kubectl get pods shows a pod with STATUS Running but READY 0/1. Users get no responses through the Service. What does this indicate?
o: The container is running but not ready, typically because its readiness probe is failing, so it is removed from the Service endpoints
The image can't be pulled
The node is out of disk space
The pod has been evicted
e: READY is the ratio of ready containers to total containers; a container can be running but not ready when its readiness probe fails, and Services only route to ready pods. Image pull problems show ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull, and evictions show a different status.

q: An app in AKS needs a database password. Following Kubernetes practice, how should you provide it to the container?
o: Store it in a Kubernetes Secret and reference it from the container env with secretKeyRef (or mount it as a volume)
Hard-code it in the container image
Put it in a ConfigMap and mark the ConfigMap as encrypted
Pass it as a command-line argument in the manifest
e: Secrets are the Kubernetes object for sensitive values, and containers consume them as environment variables or mounted files; missing or misconfigured Secrets and ConfigMaps are a documented cause of crashes. ConfigMaps are for non-sensitive configuration, and images or command arguments expose the value to anyone who can read them.

q: A pod in AKS shows ImagePullBackOff. What should you do first to get the detailed error?
o: Run kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <namespace> and read the Events section
Run kubectl logs <pod>
Restart the AKS cluster
Delete and recreate the namespace
e: For ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull, the Events in kubectl describe pod show why the pull failed, such as authorization errors, a missing tag, or DNS issues. kubectl logs returns nothing because the container never started, and restarting the cluster or recreating the namespace doesn't diagnose anything.

q: You suspect your AKS nodes can't reach or authenticate to your Azure container registry. Which command checks this from the cluster's perspective?
o: az aks check-acr --resource-group rg --name aks1 --acr contoso.azurecr.io
az acr check-health --name contoso only from your laptop
kubectl get nodes
az acr task logs --registry contoso
e: az aks check-acr validates that the AKS cluster can access the registry and that the kubelet identity is authorized. Checking registry health from a laptop doesn't test the cluster's network path or identity, kubectl get nodes only lists nodes, and task logs only show ACR build output.

q: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. The current container restarts too quickly to see its output. Which command shows the logs from the previous, crashed container?
o: kubectl logs <pod> -n <namespace> --previous
kubectl describe node
kubectl get events --watch-only on the Service
az aks show --query provisioningState
e: kubectl logs --previous returns the logs of the last terminated instance of the container, which usually contains the exception or error that caused the crash. Node descriptions and cluster provisioning state don't include application output.

q: A new Container Apps revision never becomes healthy. You open Log stream in the portal. Which log type shows image pull failures, probe results, and secret sync errors?
o: System logs
Console logs
HTTP logs
Activity log
e: System logs contain platform events such as image pull status, probe results, identity errors, and secret sync outcomes. Console logs contain your application's stdout and stderr. HTTP logs record ingress requests, and the Activity log records management operations on the resource.

q: Your container apps send logs to Log Analytics. Which tables hold the application output and the platform events?
o: ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL for stdout/stderr and ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL for system events
AppRequests and AppDependencies
ContainerLogV2 and KubeEvents
AzureActivity and Heartbeat
e: Container Apps writes console output to ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL and system events to ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL when the environment uses Log Analytics (or the equivalent tables without the suffix when using diagnostic settings). ContainerLogV2 and KubeEvents belong to AKS Container insights, and AppRequests holds Application Insights request telemetry.

q: When you open Log stream for a container app, the portal says the revision is scaled to zero. What should you do to see live logs?
o: Make the revision run a replica, for example by sending a request or setting the minimum replicas to 1
Switch to the Logs blade; it streams logs from scaled-to-zero revisions
Delete the revision
Disable ingress
e: Log streaming shows output from running replicas. If the revision is scaled to zero there is nothing to stream, so the troubleshooting guide suggests deploying or configuring the revision with a minimum replica count (or generating traffic). Historical logs are queried in Log Analytics, not streamed, and disabling ingress doesn't start a replica.

q: A container app revision is Degraded with 0 ready replicas, and system logs show the probe gets connection refused. What should you check first?
o: That the probe port matches the port the app listens on and the ingress targetPort
That the Log Analytics workspace exists
That the app is in multiple revision mode
That the registry is geo-replicated
e: Connection refused means nothing is listening on the probed port. The deployment troubleshooting guide says to set the probe port to match the app's listening port and the ingress target port, and to increase delays if the app starts slowly. Logging destination, revision mode, and geo-replication don't cause probe connection failures.

q: You didn't configure any health probes, but a slow-starting container app keeps restarting with startup probe failures. Why?
o: When ingress is enabled and no probes are defined, Container Apps applies default probes against the target port
Container Apps always runs a probe on port 80 regardless of ingress
Probes are created by the KEDA scaler
The container image contains a HEALTHCHECK that Container Apps converts to a liveness probe
e: With ingress enabled and no probes configured, Container Apps adds default probes that target the ingress target port. A slow-starting app can fail them, so define your own startup probe with suitable delays and thresholds. KEDA doesn't create probes, and the platform doesn't use the Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK.

q: AKS has Container insights enabled. In which Log Analytics table do you query container stdout/stderr logs using the recommended schema?
o: ContainerLogV2
ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL
AppTraces
AzureDiagnostics
e: Container insights stores the container logs it collects from AKS in the ContainerLogV2 table, the recommended schema with fields such as PodName, PodNamespace, and ContainerName. ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL is for Azure Container Apps, AppTraces is Application Insights log telemetry, and AzureDiagnostics holds resource logs from many services.

q: You need the logs of every container belonging to pods whose names contain checkout in the last hour. ContainerLogV2 alone isn't enough because you also want pod inventory details. Which pair of tables does Microsoft's sample query join?
o: KubePodInventory and ContainerLogV2 on ContainerID
KubeEvents and AppRequests on operation_Id
ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL and KubePodInventory on RevisionName
Heartbeat and Perf on Computer
e: The Container insights sample joins KubePodInventory (pod name, namespace, container ID) with ContainerLogV2 on ContainerID to return log lines for matching pods. operation_Id is an Application Insights correlation field, and the Container Apps and VM tables don't contain AKS pod inventory.

q: You need to run commands inside a running container app replica to check DNS resolution to a database. What should you use?
o: The container console (for example az containerapp exec)
Log stream
Azure Monitor metrics
Revision labels
e: Container Apps provides a container console so you can connect to the shell inside a running container and debug from there. Log stream only shows output, metrics show resource usage, and labels give a revision its own FQDN.
